subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Skeletal muscle fiber types and adaptations
vignette: A muscle biopsy is taken from the soleus of a trained long-distance runner. The examined fibers are red, contract slowly, are fatigue resistant, and contain abundant mitochondria and myoglobin. The fibers are well suited to sustained, aerobic activity.
question: Which of the following best describes this fiber type?

options.text: Type I fibers: slow, red, oxidative phosphorylation, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, suited to sustained contraction
Type II fibers: fast, white, anaerobic glycolysis, suited to sprinting
Type II fibers: fast, red, oxidative phosphorylation, fatigue resistant
Type I fibers: fast, white, anaerobic glycolysis, suited to weight lifting
Type II fibers: slow, red, oxidative phosphorylation, rich in myoglobin

explanation_correct: Type I fibers are slow-twitch, red fibers that rely predominantly on oxidative phosphorylation. Their red color comes from abundant myoglobin and a rich capillary and mitochondrial content, which supports aerobic ATP production and resistance to fatigue. They are specialized for sustained, low-intensity contraction such as endurance running. The mnemonic is '1 slow red ox.'

explanation_incorrect.B: This describes type II fibers, which are fast, pale, glycolytic, and suited to brief intense efforts rather than sustained aerobic contraction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Type II fibers are not the fatigue-resistant, mitochondria-rich fibers described; that profile belongs to type I fibers.
explanation_incorrect.D: This reverses the properties: type I fibers are slow and oxidative, not fast and glycolytic, and weight lifting relies on type II fibers.
explanation_incorrect.E: Type II fibers are not slow, red, and mitochondria-rich; those are type I characteristics.

educationalObjective: Type I fibers are slow, red, oxidative, mitochondria- and myoglobin-rich, and optimized for sustained endurance contraction.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Skeletal muscle fiber types and adaptations
vignette: A sprinter undergoes a biopsy of the gastrocnemius. The sampled fibers are pale, contract rapidly, fatigue quickly, and have relatively few mitochondria and little myoglobin. Their dominant metabolic pathway is anaerobic glycolysis.
question: Which of the following best characterizes these fibers and the training that favors them?

options.text: Type I fibers relying on anaerobic glycolysis, recruited during sprinting
Type II fibers that are red because of abundant myoglobin and mitochondria
Type I fibers with few mitochondria that fatigue rapidly
Type II fibers relying on anaerobic glycolysis, favored by sprinting and resistance training
Type II fibers specialized for sustained, low-intensity endurance activity

explanation_correct: Type II fibers are fast-twitch, pale ('white') fibers that depend predominantly on anaerobic glycolysis. They have fewer mitochondria and less myoglobin than type I fibers, so they fatigue rapidly but generate force quickly and powerfully. They are recruited for sprinting and weight/resistance training. The mnemonic is '2 fast white antelopes.'

explanation_incorrect.A: Anaerobic glycolysis and sprinting are associated with type II, not type I, fibers; type I fibers are oxidative and endurance-oriented.
explanation_incorrect.B: Type II fibers are pale, not red, because they contain relatively little myoglobin and fewer mitochondria.
explanation_incorrect.C: Type I fibers are mitochondria-rich and fatigue resistant, so this description is the opposite of the type I phenotype.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sustained, low-intensity endurance activity is the domain of type I oxidative fibers, not type II glycolytic fibers.

educationalObjective: Type II fibers are fast, white, glycolytic, and fatigue-prone, and are favored by sprint and resistance training.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Skeletal muscle fiber types and adaptations
vignette: A 34-year-old man sustains a peripheral nerve injury that denervates a portion of a muscle. Several months later, a biopsy of the affected region shows clusters of adjacent fibers that are all the same histochemical type, rather than the normal random intermixture of type I and type II fibers.
question: Which of the following best explains this finding of muscle fiber type grouping?

options.text: The normal random distribution of fiber types within a healthy muscle
Reinnervation of denervated fibers after peripheral nerve damage, in which a surviving motor neuron adopts fibers of a single type
Increased mitochondrial biogenesis from endurance training alone
Selective apoptosis of myonuclei within the affected fibers
Fusion of satellite cells with existing fibers during hypertrophy

explanation_correct: Fiber types are normally distributed randomly within a muscle because motor units are intermixed. After peripheral nerve damage, denervated muscle fibers can be reinnervated by sprouting axons of surviving motor neurons. Because a single motor neuron determines the fiber type of all the fibers it supplies, the reinnervated fibers become converted to one type, producing the characteristic grouping of like fibers on biopsy. Fiber type grouping is therefore a hallmark of prior denervation with reinnervation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Normal muscle shows a random checkerboard mixture of fiber types, not clustering of identical fiber types.
explanation_incorrect.C: Endurance training increases mitochondrial content within existing fibers but does not produce the clustered, single-type groupings of reinnervation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Apoptosis of myonuclei occurs in atrophy and reduces nuclear number, but it does not create fiber type grouping.
explanation_incorrect.E: Satellite cell fusion adds myonuclei during hypertrophy and repair, but it is not the mechanism that converts groups of fibers to a uniform type.

educationalObjective: Muscle fiber type grouping results from reinnervation of denervated fibers after peripheral nerve injury, since one motor neuron imposes a single fiber type.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Skeletal muscle fiber types and adaptations
vignette: A 70-year-old woman with severe osteoarthritis has disuse atrophy of her quadriceps after months of reduced mobility. A biopsy shows smaller fibers with fewer contractile elements and fewer nuclei than normal.
question: Which of the following best describes the changes occurring in this atrophied skeletal muscle?

options.text: Increased myofibrils arranged in parallel and increased myonuclei
Increased myonuclei from satellite cell fusion with unchanged myofibrils
Decreased myofibrils but increased myonuclei from satellite cell fusion
No change in myofibrils or myonuclei, only a change in fiber type
Decreased myofibrils via the ubiquitin–proteasome system and decreased myonuclei via apoptosis

explanation_correct: Muscle atrophy involves net loss of contractile protein and nuclei. Myofibrillar proteins are degraded primarily through the ubiquitin–proteasome system, reducing the number of myofibrils. In addition, myonuclei are lost through selective apoptosis, so the atrophied fiber has fewer nuclei. This contrasts with hypertrophy, in which sarcomeres are added in parallel and satellite cell fusion increases myonuclear number.

explanation_incorrect.A: Increased parallel myofibrils and increased myonuclei describe hypertrophy, the opposite of atrophy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Satellite cell fusion adding myonuclei occurs in hypertrophy and repair, not in disuse atrophy, and myofibrils are not unchanged.
explanation_incorrect.C: In atrophy, myonuclei decrease through apoptosis rather than increase through satellite cell fusion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atrophy clearly changes fiber size, myofibril content, and nuclear number; it is not merely a fiber-type shift.

educationalObjective: Skeletal muscle atrophy decreases myofibrils through ubiquitin–proteasome degradation and decreases myonuclei through apoptosis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Skeletal muscle fiber types and adaptations
vignette: A 24-year-old bodybuilder has markedly enlarged biceps from years of resistance training. A biopsy shows an increased number of myofibrils packed within each fiber and an increased number of nuclei located at the fiber periphery.
question: Which of the following best describes the cellular basis of this skeletal muscle hypertrophy?

options.text: Addition of sarcomeres in series only, with no change in myonuclei
Removal of myofibrils by the ubiquitin–proteasome system
Addition of sarcomeres in parallel (more myofibrils) and fusion of satellite cells that increases myonuclei
Selective apoptosis of myonuclei with enlarged remaining fibers
Conversion of type I fibers to type II fibers without new protein synthesis

explanation_correct: Skeletal muscle hypertrophy results from increased synthesis of contractile proteins, with sarcomeres added in parallel so that the number of myofibrils within each fiber increases and the fiber enlarges in cross-sectional diameter. Because mature myonuclei are postmitotic, additional nuclei are supplied by satellite cells, which fuse with the fiber and donate their nuclei to support the greater protein synthetic demand. This distinguishes hypertrophy from atrophy at the cellular level.

explanation_incorrect.A: Addition of sarcomeres in series would lengthen fibers rather than increase their girth, and hypertrophy does increase myonuclear number via satellite cells.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ubiquitin–proteasome degradation of myofibrils causes atrophy, not hypertrophy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Apoptosis of myonuclei occurs in atrophy; hypertrophy adds nuclei through satellite cell fusion.
explanation_incorrect.E: A pure fiber-type conversion without new protein synthesis cannot account for the increased myofibril and nuclear content seen in true hypertrophy.

educationalObjective: Hypertrophy adds sarcomeres in parallel and increases myonuclei through satellite cell fusion, enlarging fiber cross-sectional area.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Skeletal muscle fiber types and adaptations
vignette: A comparative physiologist is contrasting regenerative capacity in skeletal and cardiac muscle after injury. In skeletal muscle, satellite cells activate, proliferate, and fuse with damaged fibers to repair them and add myonuclei. She notes that this satellite-cell-mediated mechanism is notably absent in the heart, which instead forms scar tissue after myocardial infarction.
question: Which of the following best explains the limited regenerative capacity of cardiac muscle compared with skeletal muscle?

options.text: Cardiac muscle lacks satellite cells, so it cannot regenerate by satellite cell fusion the way skeletal muscle can
Cardiac muscle contains abundant satellite cells that fuse with cardiomyocytes after injury
Skeletal muscle lacks satellite cells, whereas cardiac muscle relies on them for repair
Satellite cells are present in both tissues but are inactive only in skeletal muscle
Satellite cells are a specialized type of myonucleus found exclusively in cardiac muscle

explanation_correct: Satellite cells are a reserve population of myogenic stem cells located between the sarcolemma and basement membrane of skeletal muscle fibers. They fuse with existing fibers to repair damaged myofibrils and to supply additional myonuclei during hypertrophy. These cells are absent in cardiac muscle, which is a key reason injured myocardium heals by fibrosis and scar formation rather than by true regeneration of contractile tissue.

explanation_incorrect.B: Cardiac muscle does not contain the satellite cells that mediate skeletal muscle regeneration; this is why myocardial injury results in scarring.
explanation_incorrect.C: This reverses the distribution: satellite cells are a feature of skeletal muscle and are absent in cardiac muscle.
explanation_incorrect.D: Satellite cells are active in skeletal muscle repair and hypertrophy; they are the cells missing in cardiac muscle.
explanation_incorrect.E: Satellite cells are not myonuclei; they are distinct stem cells, and they are not found exclusively in cardiac muscle.

educationalObjective: Satellite cells mediate skeletal muscle repair and hypertrophy by fusing with fibers, but they are absent in cardiac muscle, limiting cardiac regeneration.
